summary: For ages 9–10 (NGSS 4-ESS3-1): energy and fuels come from natural resources, and using them affects the environment. Children distinguish renewable sources (wind, solar, water behind dams) from non-renewable ones (fossil fuels, fissile materials) using the replenishment-timescale criterion, and weigh the environmental trade-offs of each. The target science practice is obtaining and combining information from more than one source, so the strongest work has learners compare real information about impacts rather than accept 'renewables good, others bad'. Activities span an energy-mix decision bench, an in-role debate that exercises combining evidence, and a sorting/matching classification check.
misconceptions: Renewable simply means 'clean with no downsides' — renewables have impacts too (land use, dam habitat loss, intermittency)
Fossil fuels will 'never run out' or renew quickly — they form over millions of years and are effectively finite
Electricity is itself a fuel/resource — it is a carrier generated from a primary resource
Any environmentally friendly choice fixes every problem at once
Nuclear is 'renewable' — fissile material is a non-renewable resource

activities.title: Power your town: an energy-mix decision bench
steps: Allocate an energy mix to keep a town's lights on, dragging in options such as coal, gas, wind, solar and hydro to meet demand.

Watch each choice's consequences update: a coal plant gives steady power, but the sky greys with smoke pollution, invisible CO₂ builds up, and its fuel bar drains toward empty; wind and solar make no air pollution while running but need many units and sag when the weather turns or (for solar) at night; a dam delivers fairly steady power but floods a valley.
Switch the town fully off fossil fuels and observe what changes — the air clears and the fuel gauges stop draining, but far more renewable capacity is needed and output dips with the weather.
State in your own words which sources refill on a human timescale and which run out, and name one environmental trade-off for each source you used.
activities.insight: Renewable vs non-renewable is about whether the source refills on a human timescale, and every source carries an environmental trade-off rather than being simply 'good' or 'bad'.

activities.title: Obtain and combine: energy-engineer debate
steps: Take the role of an energy engineer, or hold a debate between an energy-company voice and an environmentalist, and gather information about a chosen energy source from more than one source of information.
Combine the information to describe how extracting and using that source affects the environment (for example fossil-fuel air pollution and CO₂, dam or mining habitat loss).
Justify a recommended resource choice by its environmental effects, acknowledging at least one downside of the option you favour.
activities.insight: The 4-ESS3-1 practice is obtaining and combining information from multiple sources and weighing competing evidence to justify a position about resource use.

activities.title: Sort and match: renewable, non-renewable, and their impacts
steps: Sort energy resources (coal, oil, gas, wind, sun, water) into renewable vs non-renewable using the replenishment criterion.
Match each resource to its characteristic environmental effect (e.g. burning fossil fuels → air pollution and CO₂; dams → habitat loss by flooding; surface mining → habitat loss).
Decide the two tricky classification cases: whether nuclear/fissile material is renewable, and whether electricity is a primary resource.
Given a new source not practised, classify it by whether it refills on a human timescale.
activities.insight: Renewable/non-renewable is defined by whether the resource naturally replenishes on a human timescale, which is separate from how clean it is and separate from electricity (a carrier, not a resource).

checkQuestion: Wind turbines and coal power stations both make electricity. One uses a renewable resource and one a non-renewable resource. Which is which — and what does 'renewable' actually mean about that resource?
checkAnswer: Wind is renewable, coal is non-renewable. Renewable means the resource is naturally replenished on a human timescale and won't run out from use (wind, sunlight, flowing water); non-renewable means there's a finite amount that took millions of years to form and gets used up (coal, oil, gas). Renewable doesn't mean 'no environmental impact,' but non-renewable fossil fuels release CO₂ and pollution when burned.
